Feature weighting and data nuggets

Source: vignettes/articles/weighting-and-nuggets.Rmd
weighting-and-nuggets.Rmd

Not every feature carries signal, and not every source deserves equal weight. MosaiClusteR lets you weight both. This page covers feature weighting inside the M-ABC family, the data-nugget scheme behind it, and source weighting across the integration.

Feature weighting in M-ABC

The M-ABC family repeats, per source: bootstrap the samples, draw a weighted subsample of features, cluster, and record co-clustering. The probability that a feature is drawn comes from a weighting scheme:

weighting Score behind the selection probability Best when
"var" feature variance (the classic choice) signal lives in high-variance features
"cv" coefficient of variation you want a scale-free measure of spread
"nugget" data-nugget between-group weighted variance large N, heavy tails, outliers
"equal" flat weights an ablation, or no prior on features 
library(MosaiClusteR)
data(mosaic_toy)
L <- mosaic_toy$List

M_ABC(L, NC = 3, weighting = c("var", "var"))                 # variance weighting
M_ABC(L, NC = 3, weighting = c("nugget", "nugget"), seed = 1) # nugget weighting

Pass one weighting per source. Variance weighting is a sound default; switch to "nugget" when a few extreme observations would otherwise dominate the variance.

Data nuggets

A data nugget summarises a group of observations by three numbers: a centre, a weight (how many observations it stands for), and a scale (its internal spread). Compressing the objects into nuggets and asking which features separate the nugget centres gives a feature-importance score that rewards real between-group signal and discounts within-nugget noise. Because it works on a small set of representatives, it scales to very large N.

dn <- create_data_nuggets(L[[1]], max_nuggets = 25)   # objects are in rows
dn                                                    # reports the compression
w  <- nugget_feature_weights(dn, type = "between")    # one weight per feature
head(sort(w, decreasing = TRUE))

nugget_feature_weights() offers different notions of importance through type: "between" rewards separation of the nugget centres, while other options weigh within-group spread. The "between" weights are the ones M-ABC uses when weighting = "nugget".

Two engines build the nuggets. The built-in native engine needs no extra package. If the reference datanugget package is installed, pass engine = "datanugget" to use it instead:

create_data_nuggets(L[[1]], max_nuggets = 25, engine = "datanugget")

You can also pass nugget options straight into M-ABC with nugget_args:

M_ABC(L, NC = 3, weighting = c("nugget", "nugget"),
      nugget_args = list(max_nuggets = 25, seed = 1))

Clustering the nuggets directly

For big-data clustering, cluster the compressed representatives and map the labels back to the objects. nugget_cluster() does the whole round trip; Wkmeans() and Whclust() are the weighted k-means and weighted Ward primitives underneath.

nugget_cluster(do.call(cbind, L), k = 3, max_nuggets = 40)$cluster
Wkmeans(dn, k = 3)
Whclust(dn, k = 3)

simulate_weighting_regime() generates data under a known weighting regime, which is useful for checking how each scheme behaves before applying it to real data.

Source weighting

Feature weighting decides which columns matter; source weighting decides which sources matter. Two routes:

  • A weight grid. WeightedClust() forms a convex combination of the per-source distances over a grid of weights, so you can see how the solution changes as one source gains influence.
  • Data-driven weights. DetermineWeight_SilClust() and DetermineWeight_SimClust() pick source weights from silhouette or similarity criteria, so the data chooses the balance.
WeightedClust(L, type = "data", distmeasure = rep("euclidean", length(L)),
              normalize = rep(FALSE, length(L)), method = rep(list(NULL), length(L)),
              weight = seq(1, 0, -0.1))
DetermineWeight_SilClust(L, type = "data")
